question: What age group is classified as adolescents in public health data?
explanation: Adolescence spans the second decade of life, specifically from ages 10 to 19, according to standard health definitions. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why do female adolescents contract HIV at higher rates than their male peers?

options.A: Complete absence of immune cells in the female mucosa
options.B: Higher rates of intravenous drug use among young women
options.C: Biological susceptibility and gender power imbalances
options.D: Genetic mutations exclusive to the female X chromosome

explanation: Young women face higher risk due to a larger mucosal surface area for exposure and social inequalities that make negotiating safe sex difficult. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h1)

question: What anatomical feature increases biological vulnerability to STIs in young females?
explanation: Cervical ectopy exposes immature cells to pathogens, making it easier for infections to take hold. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h2)

question: How does adolescent brain development influence sexual health risk?

options.A: Enhanced ability to calculate long-term epidemiological risks
options.B: Permanent impairment of verbal communication skills
options.C: Complete loss of memory regarding safe sex practices
options.D: Delayed prefrontal cortex maturation promotes impulsive decision-making

explanation: The part of the brain responsible for impulse control and risk assessment matures slowly during the teen years. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h2)

question: What is a major long-term complication of untreated chlamydia and gonorrhea in young women?
explanation: Infections that travel upward can cause inflammation and scarring in the fallopian tubes, which affects future fertility. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h3)

question: How do genital ulcers from infections like syphilis and herpes make it easier to acquire HIV?

options.A: They increase systemic body temperature to lethal levels
options.B: They actively destroy white blood cells throughout the entire body
options.C: They create breaks in mucosal or skin barriers for viral entry
options.D: They release toxins that paralyze the immune system permanently

explanation: Sores and breaks in the skin or mucosal lining give the virus direct access to underlying blood vessels and immune cells. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h3)

question: Which specific immune cells are primarily targeted and destroyed by the HIV virus?
explanation: HIV attaches to CD4 receptors to enter host T-cells, weakening the body's immune defenses as it replicates. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h4)

question: What marks the transition from asymptomatic HIV infection to advanced AIDS?

options.A: Severe opportunistic infections and profound CD4 cell depletion
options.B: Sudden permanent normalization of white blood cell counts
options.C: Development of immunity without any medical intervention
options.D: Complete disappearance of the virus from all bodily fluids

explanation: When CD4 counts drop very low, the weakened immune system allows opportunistic infections to take over, marking the onset of AIDS. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h4)

question: What does the window period mean in HIV testing?

options.A: The time between infection and detectable antibodies
options.B: The lifespan of an antiretroviral pill in the stomach
options.C: The duration a patient must wait before taking medication
options.D: The exact hours during the day when clinics are open

explanation: The window period is the gap of time before the body creates enough antibodies for a standard test to show a positive result. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h5)

question: A 16-year-old visits for an HIV test two days after unprotected sex. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Tell the patient they are completely free of HIV since the test is negative today
options.B: Immediately start lifelong antiretroviral therapy without waiting for any lab results
options.C: Refuse testing because adolescents are not legally permitted to test without parents
options.D: Provide counseling, perform baseline testing, and schedule a repeat test after the window period

explanation: Because of the window period, an immediate negative test does not guarantee the person is uninfected, so follow-up testing is necessary. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of starting Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) in adolescents?

options.A: Preventing the normal growth and development of bones
options.B: Achieving lifelong viral suppression and preserving immune function
options.C: Permanently curing the viral infection within two weeks
options.D: Eliminating the need for any future medical checkups

explanation: ART lowers the amount of virus in the body to very low levels, which protects CD4 cells and stops the disease from progressing to AIDS. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h6)

question: Why is taking daily medication consistently a challenge for many adolescents living with HIV?

options.A: Complete immunity to all known pharmacological drugs
options.B: Inability of adolescent kidneys to filter chemical compounds
options.C: Pill fatigue, fear of disclosure, and lifestyle disruptions
options.D: Constant medical supervision that prevents normal schooling

explanation: Managing a chronic condition while trying to fit in with peers makes keeping up with daily pills difficult for many teenagers. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is a key feature of Adolescent-Friendly Health Services (AFHS)?

options.A: High service fees to cover premium facility maintenance
options.B: Mandatory notification of all school authorities upon visit
options.C: Strict adult-only operating hours on weekday mornings
options.D: Guaranteed confidentiality and non-judgmental staff attitude

explanation: Teens are more likely to seek help if they know their privacy is protected and staff will not judge them. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h7)

question: Why are peer support groups helpful for adolescents managing HIV?

options.A: They eliminate the biological viral load from the bloodstream
options.B: They replace the need for professional clinical nursing assessments
options.C: They reduce isolation and build coping strategies through shared experiences
options.D: They provide a legal authority to dispense prescription medications

explanation: Talking with other young people facing similar health situations helps normalize their experience and supports better treatment habits. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h7)

question: Which medication approach helps prevent HIV infection in individuals at high risk?
explanation: PrEP involves taking antiretroviral medications beforehand to lower the chances of contracting HIV if exposed. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h8)

question: How does reducing community stigma directly help adolescent health outcomes?

options.A: It guarantees financial employment for all infected individuals
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future clinical research studies
options.C: It encourages early testing, open disclosure, and consistent treatment adherence
options.D: It automatically cures active bacterial and viral infections

explanation: When fear of discrimination goes down, adolescents feel safer getting tested and sticking to their medications. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T15#GNS312_U3_T15_h8)
